transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, I’m here because... honestly, it’s all just become too much, and I needed someone to understand what’s really going on. I came in because I finally realized—I knew it, deep down, but I finally saw it clearly—that my in-laws, they aren’t just arguing with me anymore. It’s not just the usual bickering about Sunday dinners or how I keep the house, which, let me tell you, I have kept immaculate for thirty-five years. No, it’s much bigger than that now. They’re actually using the altar at the church, and the entire parish committee—people I’ve known for decades, people I’ve baked pies for!—they’re using them to push me out. It’s a whole orchestrated thing to make everyone completely forget everything I have done for this family. All the sacrifices, all the late nights, the holidays I hosted... they want to erase me, and they’re using the church to do it. And I just couldn't sit at home and let them get away with it without telling someone who might actually listen to the truth.
When you say your in-laws and the parish committee are trying to erase you, do you believe this is part of a deliberate and organized plan against you, even if others don’t see it that way?

Oh, absolutely. It is completely deliberate. Like I was just saying, this isn't just them being difficult or having a little family spat with me. I know—I know in my bones—that they are using the altar and the whole parish committee to push me out. 

You ask if others don't see it... well, of course they don't see it! My husband, bless his heart, he’s totally blind to it. He just thinks, oh, it's just church politics, don't worry about it, let it roll off your back. But it’s not just politics! I know for a fact that they sit around after Sunday service—probably right there in the fellowship hall, drinking the coffee I bought for the church pantry, mind you—and they plot exactly how to make everyone forget what I've done for this family. 

They whisper to the choir director, they give each other these little looks during the bake sales, all to erase me. It is a highly organized campaign, doctor. You have to understand, when you've been part of a family and a parish for as long as I have, you notice when the wind changes. You notice when the committee suddenly stops asking for your input on the Easter floral arrangements, which I have organized beautifully since 1998! It’s all part of this... this master plan to push me out and act like I never contributed a single thing to any of their lives. So yes, it is very deliberate, even if everyone else around me is walking around with their eyes glued shut. They think I'm just making a fuss, but I see exactly what they're doing.
Have you considered that others may not see this as a deliberate plan because it’s not actually happening the way you believe it is?

Well, how could I consider that? How could I possibly think it's not happening when I see it with my own two eyes, every single Sunday, every single family gathering? You’re asking me to doubt my own reality, doctor, and I just can't do that. I mean, think about it from my perspective. I've spent thirty-five years—thirty-five years!—building a life, raising children, keeping a home that you could eat off the floors of, and serving that church. I was the one who suggested we switch to the silk lilies for the winter services because the real ones were wilting too fast near the radiators! 

And now, you want me to think that maybe I'm just imagining that they're using the altar against me? That the parish committee isn't involved? It’s not just in my head! I told you, I came in here because I finally realized, I *knew* it, that my in-laws aren't just having a little disagreement with me. They are actively, deliberately using the altar and the entire parish committee to push me out. They want to completely erase me and make every single person in that congregation and in this family forget what I have done for them. 

If it wasn't happening the way I believe it is, then why did Susan—my sister-in-law, who I taught how to make a proper pie crust, by the way—why did she look right past me when they were handing out the bulletins last week? Why did the head of the committee suddenly decide that they didn't need my help organizing the spring bazaar? I've run that bazaar for over a decade! We raised enough money for a new roof in 2012 because of my silent auction idea! You don't just 'forget' to ask someone who did all that, unless it's on purpose. Unless you're trying to push them out. 

So no, I don't think I'm wrong. I don't think it's just me misunderstanding things. People don't want to see it because it's ugly, doctor. It's an ugly truth that people who smile at you and take communion with you could be plotting to erase your entire legacy. My husband doesn't want to see it because it means confronting his own family, and he hates conflict. He’d rather just watch his golf and pretend everything is fine. But I can't pretend. I know what they're doing with the committee, I know what they're doing at the altar, and I know they want me gone and forgotten.
Have you taken any steps to address what you believe is happening, like confronting your in-laws or speaking to someone in the church about it?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean... how could I? Who on earth would I even go to? If I go to the church leadership, who am I going to talk to? Father Thomas? Please! He’s been having dinner at my sister-in-law Susan’s house every third Sunday for the last five years! I used to be the one making the roast for those dinners, you know. A beautiful rump roast with carrots and potatoes, cooked low and slow all afternoon, and my gravy—well, people used to ask for the recipe, but I never gave it out. But now? Now he’s over there eating her dry, overcooked chicken and probably listening to her poison him against me. So I certainly can't go to him, because he's already under their spell. 

And confront my in-laws directly? Oh, I’ve thought about it. Believe me, I have sat in my living room, in my favorite floral armchair—the one I had reupholstered back in 2015, it’s a lovely cream and burgundy damask, very tasteful—and I have rehearsed exactly what I would say to them. I’ve gone over it a hundred times in my head. I’d march right up and say, "I see what you’re doing with the altar, and I see what you're doing with the committee!" But... if I actually say it out loud to them, they’ll just do exactly what you just tried to do, doctor. They’ll tell me I’m making things up. They’ll use it as more ammunition. 

They *want* me to make a scene. That’s part of the plan, don’t you see? If I march up to the parish committee during their Wednesday night bingo prep—and by the way, I was the one who organized the prize baskets for bingo for years, driving all over town getting donations from the local businesses down on Main Street, spending my own gas money—if I go down there and confront them, they’ll just look at each other, give those little knowing nods, and say, "Oh, look at her, she’s making a fuss again." That is exactly what they want! They want me to look unstable so they have an excuse to erase me completely and justify everything they've been doing behind my back. 

So, no. I haven't given them the satisfaction. I haven't said a single word to them about it because I know better than to walk right into their trap. I just sit back, and I watch them. I see it all happening, and I keep track of it. Every little slight, every ignored greeting, every time they change the schedule without telling me... I see it, but I haven't confronted them because that's exactly the opening they're waiting for.
Have you ever had other beliefs or experiences that you were sure were real, but others told you weren’t true or didn’t make sense?

Well, if you're asking if my husband thinks I'm seeing things or making things up, then yes, I suppose there is something else. But again, it’s just him being completely blind to what is right in front of his face! 

You see, I've been trying to get the house in order, especially with all this stress from the church, and I like things done a very specific way. My mother, God rest her soul, she taught me everything I know about keeping a proper home. She was an absolute stickler for details, just like me. And lately... well, on several nights recently, I've actually heard her. Clear as a bell! I was up late, probably around two or three in the morning, working on some floral arrangements for the dining room—because if I don't keep the house looking beautiful, it all just falls apart—and I heard her voice telling me exactly where to put the marigolds. Marigolds can be very tricky, you know, they have that very distinct scent and a bold color, so you have to balance them just right. And she was right there, her voice telling me exactly where the candles needed to go around them to catch the light properly. 

And then... well, there was this one time, just a few days ago, where I actually saw her. I was in the kitchen. I had just finished wiping down the counters—I always use a water and vinegar solution, by the way, it cuts through the grime so much better than those awful chemical sprays they sell at the supermarket now—and I looked up, and she was standing right there near the kitchen doorway. Just standing there! Wearing her old blue housecoat. 

I gasped, I really did, and my husband came shuffling out of the bedroom in his slippers, rubbing his eyes and grumbling about the noise. I pointed right at the doorway, right at her! And do you know what he said? He looked right at the spot, looked back at me, and told me no one was there. He told me I was just dreaming while I was awake and that it didn't make any sense. 

But I wasn't dreaming! How could I be dreaming when I was holding a damp sponge in my hand? I know my own mother's voice, and I know what I saw in my own kitchen doorway. He just doesn't pay attention to anything. He didn't see her, so suddenly it 'isn't true.' Just like he doesn't see what the parish committee is doing behind my back. It's always, 'Oh, you're just tired, go back to bed.' But I know she was there helping me with the marigolds and the candles. I know what I experienced, doctor, even if he wants to tell me it isn't real.
Have you ever had other experiences or beliefs, even before this situation with your in-laws and the church, where you were certain something was true but others insisted it wasn't?

Well, before all this nonsense with my in-laws and the church? No, I really can't say that I have. I've always been a very practical, grounded woman. You don't manage a household, raise children, and run a parish committee for decades by having your head in the clouds! I’ve always lived in the real world. 

But, you know, if you're trying to imply that I just walk around imagining things all the time, I have to stop you right there. Because I pay attention to myself, doctor, and I notice how things happen. Take my mother, for instance. Hearing her voice and seeing her in the doorway... that didn't just happen out of the blue, and it certainly isn't happening every day of my life. It really only happened during that one particular stretch of time recently. 

You see, during those weeks, I was barely sleeping at all. Maybe an hour or two a night, if that! I didn't even feel tired, though. I was just rushing around, day and night, getting the house absolutely perfect, scrubbing the baseboards, fixing the floral arrangements, because I felt—no, I was absolutely sure—that I had this incredibly special, sacred duty to fix the altar. I had to protect it from what Susan and the committee were doing, and it was all up to me. I had so much energy, just buzzing around like a bee, and that is when my mother was there. She was there guiding me because the work was so important. 

But then... well, eventually, my mood just completely dropped. It was like someone pulled the plug out of the wall. I just deflated entirely. I felt so incredibly sad, just sitting in my damask armchair for days on end, feeling this awful, crushing guilt that I hadn't done enough, that I had failed the church and let everyone down. It was a terrible, heavy feeling, just weeping over my tea. 

But the important thing is, doctor—and this is why I know I'm not just losing my mind like my husband thinks—once my mood dropped down like that, and I was just sitting there feeling guilty and miserable... I wasn't hearing my mother's voice anymore. I didn't see her standing in the kitchen in her housecoat. All of that just stopped completely. I was still sad, yes, and I still felt guilty, but I was not hearing or seeing those things anymore. It only happened when I was rushing around without sleep, trying to fulfill my duty to the altar. So it’s not just some constant madness, it was tied to that specific time.

Can you think of any other times—besides what you’ve described with your in-laws, the church, and your mother—when you were absolutely certain something was true, but no one else seemed to agree with you?

Well, let me think... yes, I suppose there was the community heritage festival late last summer. Or was it early September? No, it was definitely August, I remember because the humidity was just dreadful, absolutely ruining my hair, but I didn't even care at the time because I was so entirely focused on our family's presentation. 

You see, our family has always had a major presence at this festival, it’s practically a cornerstone of the whole town's history. But my cousins and my nieces? They were just going to throw together some cheap, store-bought decorations and maybe bake a few boxed cakes. Boxed cakes! For a heritage festival! Can you even imagine the embarrassment? 

I was horrified. And in that moment, I just... I had this absolute, crystal-clear realization. I truly believed, with every fiber of my being, that I was the only one who could save our family's traditions. I mean, nobody else had the vision, doctor. Nobody else understood the stakes! I could see exactly how it all needed to be done, down to the exact draping of our grandmother's heirloom quilts and the precise way the homemade blackberry preserves needed to be stacked on the tables to catch the afternoon sun. 

I tried to explain it to them. I sat them all down at my dining room table and I said, very clearly, that if they just listened to me—if they would just step aside, follow my instructions to the letter, and let me direct everything—the whole community event would be absolutely perfect. Not just our family's booth, but the *entire* festival! Because I knew exactly how to elevate the whole thing. I had this incredible, undeniable certainty that my ideas were exactly what the town needed to make it the most spectacular jubilee in fifty years. 

But do you think they agreed with me? Of course not. My cousin Martha actually rolled her eyes and told me I was getting "too big for my britches" and acting like I was the Queen of England. Can you imagine? I was offering them absolute perfection! I knew I was the only one capable of making it a masterpiece, I had the exact blueprint for success right there in my head, but they just looked at me like I was speaking a foreign language. They just couldn't see what I was capable of, even when I was the only one trying to save them from total mediocrity.

Have you ever experienced times when your mood was unusually high, you felt extremely energetic, or you were more talkative than usual, to the point where others might have noticed and said you were acting out of character?

Well, yes, I suppose people might say that. My husband certainly had plenty to say about my behavior, though he rarely understands the half of it! But during that time I was telling you about, when I was getting everything perfect and working on the church altar? Oh, I had so much energy, doctor, I was just... well, I was talking a mile a minute to anyone who would listen! I'd call my sister in Ohio at six in the morning just to tell her about the new brass polish I found, or how the linens needed to be starched, because it was just all so clear and exciting, you know? 

There were these days... oh, I don't even know if I can fully describe it to someone who wasn't there. There were days when I felt so bright and certain, just completely illuminated from the inside out. I felt like I finally had the answers to everything, and I was just bursting with it! I’d be chatting away, explaining my vision to the florist, the neighbors, the poor mailman who was just trying to drop off the electric bill... 

But the thing is, as wonderful and bright as I felt, it could turn sour so quickly. Because if anyone—and I mean absolutely anyone—dared to question me about the altar? If they even hinted that maybe I was doing too much, or asked why I needed three dozen white roses instead of two? Well, I would snap at them like they were insulting my whole family. I mean, I would bite their head right off! 

It felt exactly like a personal attack, like they were spitting on my mother's memory or telling me my whole life's work was a joke. I remember Susan from the committee—oh, don't even get me started on Susan again—she made some little offhand comment, just a tiny little question about why I was rearranging the altar cloths on a Tuesday, and I practically screamed at her right there in the vestibule. I just couldn't tolerate anyone getting in my way or doubting my vision when I was feeling that bright and certain. So yes, I suppose I was very talkative and energetic, but heaven help you if you interrupted my plans!
Have you ever had any other beliefs that you were absolutely sure were true, even though there was no evidence to support them and others could not understand why you believed them?

Well, I know I keep bringing them up, but the whole situation with my in-laws... people thought I was just being stubborn or difficult about the church. But it wasn't just a simple disagreement over how to run things. I knew exactly what they were doing. I mean, the whole reason I ended up coming in here in the first place was because it had all just reached a boiling point, because I realized... well, I saw it plain as day, even if no one else did. 

I knew they were not just arguing with me. It was a complete, coordinated campaign. You see, they were using the altar—the very altar I have dedicated my life to keeping pristine, the one I poured all my sweat and tears into—and they were using the parish committee to just completely push me out. 

My husband’s sister, Helen, and the rest of his side of the family... they wanted to make everyone forget what I have done for this family. And I have done everything for them, doctor! I mean, you don't just spend forty years building a life and not leave a mark. I hosted every single holiday dinner since Ronald and I were married, I raised the children, I kept the family name respectable in this town, I even nursed my father-in-law when his hip gave out! And their plan was to use my sacred duties at the church, the place where my contributions are the most visible, to just... erase me. To act like I was nobody.

My husband, he just couldn't see it. He told me I was making a mountain out of a molehill, that Helen just wanted to help with the spring cleaning at the parish. Help! Helen hasn't lifted a finger to help anyone in her entire life, she doesn't even know how to properly fold a purificator, let alone starch one! No, she was using the committee to turn the parish against me, to push me out of the family entirely, and I was absolutely, one hundred percent certain of it. Nobody else understood why I was so upset, they just looked at me like I was being dramatic, but I knew the truth. I knew they were trying to wipe away my entire legacy, and I wasn't going to just sit back and let them do it!
During the times when you felt extremely energetic and certain about your ideas, did you believe you had special abilities, powers, or a unique purpose that others did not have?

Well, like I was telling you just a few minutes ago about that heritage festival in August—and heaven knows I could go on and on about that entire ordeal—it wasn't just that I thought I had a few nice ideas for the booth. No, it was so much more profound than that. It was exactly like you said, a special purpose. I felt this... this absolute certainty, like a calling, really. 

You have to understand, my mother’s side of the family has been in this county since before the roads were even paved, and we have a very specific reputation to uphold. But when I looked around at my nieces and cousins with their cheap little decorations and their boxed cakes, I just... I truly believed, deep down in my soul, that I was the only one who could save our family's traditions. I mean, I looked at them and realized nobody else had the eye for it, nobody else had the respect for the history! 

I felt like I was uniquely chosen right then and there, like I was the only person left who could see the big picture. I knew exactly how to arrange everything, how the lighting needed to hit the jars of preserves, how the whole flow of the crowd should be directed... and I just knew, I knew beyond a shadow of a doubt, that if people would just put their silly little egos aside and listen to me, the whole community event would be perfect. Not just good, but absolutely flawless. A total masterpiece! 

I tried so hard to explain to them that I had this... this special vision that they were completely lacking. I mean, I was practically handing them the keys to the most spectacular festival this town had ever seen, because I was the only one who understood what our ancestors would have wanted. If they had just let me take the reins like I was meant to, if they had just recognized what I was capable of bringing to the table, everyone in town would have been talking about our family's presentation for generations. But they just couldn't see my purpose, doctor, they just couldn't comprehend it!
Have you ever had a period of time, lasting at least two weeks, when you felt persistently sad, hopeless, or lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?

Well, yes... and it's just such a terrible contrast, doctor, it really is. Because after all that energy I was just telling you about—the festival, the altar, all those grand plans and that absolute certainty—after all of that finally left me, it was like someone came along and pulled the plug right out of the wall. 

For weeks now, well over two weeks, I have been waking up with this heavy, heavy sadness. It's like a physical weight pressing down on my chest before I even open my eyes in the morning. I used to be up with the sun, you know, making my coffee, getting a head start on the dusting or polishing the silver before the phone even started ringing. But lately, I just lie there in the dark. I look up at the ceiling and I can't find a single reason to push the covers back. 

It's just this profound emptiness. I walk downstairs and I look around at my beautiful things, things I have spent forty years collecting and caring for, and it's like there is no joy left in my house at all. And there is certainly no joy left in me. I'll just sit there in my armchair by the window for hours, not even turning on the television or opening the blinds. I see the dust settling on the mantelpiece, and I just don't care. I don't care about the church committee anymore, I don't care what Helen is whispering to the rest of the family, I don't care about any of it. 

It’s just a completely suffocating feeling, doctor, to go from feeling so bright and capable to feeling like a hollowed-out shell in your own home. You spend your whole life building a warm, inviting place, and then suddenly you're just sitting there completely drained of every last drop of happiness... it's just miserable, truly miserable. I wouldn't wish this kind of heavy, dark feeling on my worst enemy.
Have there been times when you felt you needed much less sleep than usual, even though you still had plenty of energy and didn't feel tired?

Oh, sleep... well, that's a whole other story, doctor, it really is. It has been completely turned upside down. 

At first, back when all that business with the festival and the church committee was happening, I hardly slept a wink, and the strangest thing was, I didn't even mind! I mean, I would go to bed at maybe midnight, or even one in the morning, and by three o'clock, my eyes would just pop wide open. I was sleeping only a couple of hours, at most, but I felt absolutely fantastic. I had so much energy I didn't know what to do with it! So I would get up, right in the middle of the night while Ronald was just snoring away, and I would go down to the kitchen table, turn on the little lamp, and just start making lists. Pages and pages of lists! Lists for the altar guild, lists for the festival decorations, lists of which cousins needed to bring which preserves, lists of cleaning supplies... I just had to get it all down on paper because my mind was moving so beautifully fast and I was so ready to tackle the day. I didn't feel tired at all, not one bit. 

But now... oh, it's just a completely different nightmare. Now, I still can't sleep properly, but the energy is completely gone. Now I'll wake up hours before the sun comes up, well before dawn, and instead of hopping out of bed to organize things, I just lie there. I just lie awake in the dark, staring up at the ceiling, and my chest just feels so tight because I am just worrying and worrying. I worry about the house falling apart, I worry about what Helen is doing to my reputation at the parish, I worry about... well, everything and nothing at all. My mind just spins with all this heavy, awful dread. 

And the absolute worst part is that I never, ever feel rested anymore. Not ever. I can be in that bed for nine or ten hours, just tossing and turning and watching the clock tick by, and when the morning finally comes, I feel like I've been run over by a truck. It's just exhausting, doctor. To go from needing almost no sleep and feeling like you can conquer the world, to just lying awake in the pitch black feeling completely and utterly drained... it just takes everything out of you.
During the times when you felt extremely energetic and full of ideas, did you believe that you were better than others or that you had a special status or role that made you superior to them?

Well, yes... I suppose that’s exactly what I was getting at earlier when I brought up the festival, because... well, I don't mean to sound prideful, doctor. The Lord knows my mother raised me not to put on airs, but during those weeks? Yes. I absolutely felt like I was operating on a completely different, much higher level than everyone else around me. 

I mean, I would look at my sister-in-law Helen and my nieces, and I just thought to myself, 'You people are just completely clueless.' It wasn't just that I had good ideas, it was that I truly believed—with every fiber of my being—that I was the absolute only one who could save our family's traditions. They were going to make a complete mockery of our family name with their tacky little store-bought tablecloths and their complete lack of vision. I felt like I was the only one with the proper taste, the right pedigree, the... the intellect for it! 

I looked down at what they were doing and I just knew that I was vastly superior to them in every single way that mattered. And I kept telling them, I kept trying to get it through their thick skulls that if people would just put their own petty jealousies aside and just listened to me, the whole community event would be perfect. Not just adequate, but completely flawless! I felt like I was a master conductor surrounded by people who didn't even know how to hold their instruments, let alone play them. It was just so glaringly obvious to me that I was meant to be in charge because I was simply better equipped than any of them could ever hope to be. I could honestly go on and on about how incredibly frustrating it is to be the most capable person in the room and have to watch lesser minds try to take over... it was just agonizing to watch them fumble around when I had all the answers!

Have you ever believed, even for a short time, that you were chosen for a special mission or had abilities or importance far beyond what others around you recognized, even when they didn’t agree with you?

Well, it’s not just that they didn’t recognize my importance, doctor, or that they simply disagreed with my vision. It goes so much deeper and... well, it’s just so much more sinister than a simple disagreement. You really have to understand the history here to grasp what they were doing to me. 

I have spent forty years—ever since Ronald and I were first married—making sure our family name meant something in this town. I was the one who organized the Easter lilies, I was the one who made sure the brass was polished, I was the one who kept our reputation absolutely spotless at that church. I dedicated my life to it! 

And then... well, that is actually exactly why I came in to get help in the first place. Because I finally saw the truth of what was happening right under my nose. I knew, with absolute, terrifying certainty, that my in-laws were not just arguing with me about the festival. It wasn't just some petty family bickering over who was bringing the potato salad or what color the napkins should be, even though that's what they tried to make it look like. 

No, they were actively plotting against me. Helen and my nieces, they were deliberately using the altar and the parish committee to push me out. It was a completely calculated effort to ruin me! They were whispering to the other committee members, moving my things around in the sacristy, doing everything in their power to make everyone completely forget what I have done for this family. They wanted to erase my legacy, doctor. They wanted to take all the credit for the decades of blood, sweat, and tears I poured into that parish, and just toss me aside like yesterday's newspaper. 

And they can smile and act sweet all they want, but I saw right through it. I knew exactly what their little glances across the pews meant. It is just a terrible, terrible thing to realize that your own family is orchestrating a whole campaign to strip you of your rightful place, and I just couldn't sit by and let them erase my entire life's work without a fight.
Have you ever believed that random events, objects, or people’s actions were specifically directed at you or had special meaning for you, even if others didn’t see it that way?

Random events? Special meaning? Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm not entirely sure what you mean by random objects, doctor. Like... like thinking a stop sign is trying to tell me something, or the man on the evening news is speaking directly to me? Heavens no. I'm a perfectly rational woman, I really am. 

I don't sit in my living room looking at, oh, I don't know, the floral pattern on the wallpaper and thinking it's some sort of secret code just for me. Or thinking that a stranger crossing the street is sending me signals. That sounds like something out of one of those silly science fiction movies Ronald likes to fall asleep to on Sunday afternoons. No, no, I don't have time for that sort of nonsense, I never have. My mother always taught us to be practical, grounded people. We deal in reality. 

So no, I don't see special, mystical meanings in random, everyday things. The things I see, the things I *know* are happening to me, they aren't random at all. They are very, very specific. When my nieces leave the altar cloths wrinkled, or when Helen purposely misplaces my scheduling book, that's not a random object sending me a magical sign from the universe. It's just them being spiteful and calculated and trying to ruin my hard work. So no, nothing random. Everything that's directed at me is quite deliberate, I assure you.

Have you ever believed, even for a short time, that you had a special connection to a higher power, an important historical figure, or that you were chosen to carry out a mission that no one else could?

A special connection to a higher power? Oh, heavens, no. I mean, I am a deeply faithful woman, doctor, I won't deny that. As I told you, I've spent decades dedicating my time to the parish, making sure the brass is polished and the Easter lilies are perfectly arranged. But I certainly don't think the Lord is coming down and having a private chat with me over a cup of coffee, or... or giving me some sort of divine prophecy! 

I pray just like everyone else in the pews on a Sunday morning. I don't think I'm Joan of Arc, for goodness sake, or the Virgin Mary. There was actually a woman in our congregation back in the late nineties—Brenda, I think her name was, or maybe Barbara—who used to stand up right in the middle of Father Thomas's homily and claim the Holy Spirit was giving her special instructions about the church budget. It was just embarrassing, frankly. Completely mortifying for her poor husband, who was a very respectable man, he worked over at the bank. I would never, ever behave like that. My mother raised me to have proper reverence and to know my place in the house of God. 

And as for historical figures... no. I'm just a normal sixty-year-old woman trying to protect what she's built. I don't need to think I'm Queen Victoria or Eleanor Roosevelt to know that I am the only one capable of running the festival properly. My mission, if you even want to call it that, isn't some grand, mystical crusade assigned to me by the heavens. It's just... well, it's just common sense! It's just me trying to keep Helen and my nieces from completely destroying our family's reputation with their utter incompetence and their tacky little store-bought linens. 

So no, I don't have any strange ideas about being a prophet or a saint or anything like that. I just know my own worth here on earth, and I know exactly what my family is trying to do to me.
